title: PowerToys Settings crashes on Windows 10 launch

judgment.rationale: The reporter's Event Viewer/host tracing identifies a COR_E_EXECUTIONENGINE failure before PowerToys logs are created and reports recovery after Windows servicing or a per-program CET mitigation override. Current evidence indicates a Windows/.NET CET compatibility condition rather than a confirmed PowerToys source path.
evidence: The issue reproduces on the reporter's Windows 10 system but not their Windows 11 laptop.
The reporter records exception code 0x80131506 in KERNELBASE.dll and says the process dies before PowerToys logging.
The reporter reports that updating Windows or disabling Hardware-enforced Stack Protection for PowerToys.Settings.exe resolves the crash.
The repository's local UI-test guidance records that .NET 10 CET support requires Windows 10 1904x.5007 or newer and cites the same 0x80131506 failure class.
judgment.recommended_action: Request the exact serviced Windows build and the result after current updates with the per-program override removed; do not propose a PowerToys source fix unless the runtime crash persists.

fix_assessment.rationale: The evidence supports an OS/runtime servicing dependency, and no PowerToys code change can be selected responsibly without a current fully patched Windows 10 reproduction.

issue_context.summary: Settings exits immediately on one Windows 10 environment before PowerToys logging, while the reporter says Windows updates or disabling a CET mitigation restores launch.
known_information: The reporter uses PowerToysUserSetup-0.101.2432.0-x64 and can launch Settings on a Windows 11 laptop.
Event Viewer reports COR_E_EXECUTIONENGINE exception code 0x80131506 in KERNELBASE.dll.
The crash occurs before PowerToys logs are generated.
The reporter describes both an exploit-protection workaround and success after current Windows updates.
inferences: The failure is likely below the Settings application code, in the Windows/.NET CET compatibility layer.
A fully serviced Windows 10 build may resolve the problem without a PowerToys implementation change.
issue_context.analysis: The supplied stack/crash description and the absence of product logs point to runtime initialization, not Settings application control flow. Repository test-environment guidance independently documents a Windows 10 CET servicing floor for the same exception class. The remaining decision is whether the reporter's system is still below that floor after a reboot and without the local workaround.
initial_investigation: Read the entire issue and discussion, including the reporter's Event Viewer, ProcMon, and .NET CoreHost tracing summary.
Reviewed .github/skills/ui-tests-local-vm/references/setup.md, which documents 0x80131506 for Windows 10 systems below the .NET CET servicing floor.
Checked current upstream references and fork traces; no linked PowerToys fix, duplicate resolution, or fork implementation was found.

information_gaps.information: The exact Windows 10 version, full OS build, and installed cumulative update after reboot, plus the launch result with the per-program Hardware-enforced Stack Protection override removed.
information_gaps.why_needed: It establishes whether the system still falls below the documented OS servicing requirement or whether a current supported system reproduces a PowerToys-specific crash.
information_gaps.how_to_collect: Run winver, install all offered Windows Updates, reboot, remove the PowerToys.Settings.exe Program settings override, then launch Settings from the tray icon once.

actions.label: Request Windows servicing result

comment.body: Thanks for documenting the 0x80131506 crash and the CET workaround. Because the crash occurs before PowerToys logging and you reported that Windows updates resolve it, please provide the exact Windows 10 version and full build from `winver`, plus the installed cumulative update after rebooting. Then remove the per-program Hardware-enforced Stack Protection override for PowerToys.Settings.exe and report whether launching Settings from the tray icon still crashes. This will tell us whether a current serviced system still has a PowerToys-specific problem.
